name: Juan D'Arienzo
notes: Instrumentals 1935-1939 (Biagi on piano 1935-38) are the universal opener/peak material; Echagüe 1938-39 vocal tandas and 1950s Echagüe/Laborde for peaks; Mauré 1940-44 for warm emotional middle. 1960s material very fast, use late milongas only. Milongas and valses are among the strongest in the repertoire. Best: 1935-1939 instrumental, 1938-1939 Echagüe, 1940-1944 Mauré, 1949-1957 Echagüe/Laborde

name: Carlos Di Sarli
notes: The most 'elastic' orchestra for placement: 1939-45 Rufino/Podestá for the build; 1940s instrumentals gentle; 1951-58 instrumentals (Bahía Blanca, A la gran muñeca, El amanecer) for peak/late and for grand endings. Keep 1940s and 1950s recordings in separate tandas (fidelity and tempo differ). Valses excellent; milongas few but usable (Zorzal, La mulateada). Best: 1939-1943 Rufino, 1942-1944 Podes

name: Aníbal Troilo
notes: 1941-1943 (Fiorentino) is core golden-age material, mid-energy, elastic phrasing. 1944-47 Marino 'demands more' than Fiorentino (Lavocah) - for experienced floors, middle/peak. Instrumentals 1941 (Cachirulo, Milongueando en el 40, Guapeando) are peak rhythmic Troilo. Post-1950 and the 'Últimos instrumentales' mostly lack the beat for social dancing. subPeriods.note: instrumentals from 1950 on are concert repertoire unless whitelisted

nonDanceTitles: Selección de temas de Francisco Canaro

name: Osvaldo Pugliese
notes: Instrumentals 1946-1959 (La yumba, Gallo ciego, Pata ancha, Negracha, Malandraca, Nochero soy, A Evaristo Carriego) are the universal peak tanda. Never in the first hour; one tanda per 4 h; never adjacent to alternative music; follow with vals/milonga or light rhythmic tango. Rubato and arrastre make difficulty high: for beginner floors use 1943-46 Chanel vocals instead. Valses (Desde el alma 1947

name: Miguel Caló
notes: Vocal tandas (few danceable instrumentals - build vocal). Elegant, balanced, mid-tempo; ideal for the second hour and for the sweet ending. 1942-43 Berón/Podestá/Iriarte is the core. Valses (Pedacito de cielo, Bajo un cielo de estrellas) are classics. Best: 1941-1943, 1944-1946
signatureTracks: Qué te importa que te llore (Berón 1942)

name: Ricardo Tanturi
notes: Two distinct profiles: Castillo 1940-43 = rhythmic, energy ~70, early/build/peak; Campos 1943-46 = lyrical, energy ~55, middle/late. Never mix the two singers. Valses and milongas with Castillo are excellent lifts. Best: 1940-1943 Castillo, 1943-1946 Campos

name: Rodolfo Biagi
notes: Syncopated, staccato piano; feels faster than it is. Instrumentals 1938-1942 and Ortiz vocals for build/peak; valses (Lágrimas y sonrisas, Loca de amor, Dichas que viví) are the most whirling in the canon - peak vals tanda. Not for warm-up with beginners (off-beat accents confuse). Milongas strong. Best: 1938-1940 Falgás/instrumental, 1940-1943 Ortiz, 1944-1948 Amor

name: Enrique Rodríguez
notes: Square, bouncy, foxtrot-tinged; easiest music to dance in the canon; excellent warm-up and 'breathing' tandas. Valses (Tengo mil novias, Isabelita, Fru fru) and milongas are festival staples. Do not place at the main peak. Best: 1938-1945 Moreno

name: Francisco Canaro
notes: Canaro-Maida 1935-38 = gentle lyrical-rhythmic, the perfect 'easier' tanda and sweet-ending material (Poema, Invierno). Canaro-Famá 1932-36 = cheerful early. Instrumentals 1927-34 (Guardia Vieja) for warm-up and afternoon. Canaro's milongas (Milonga sentimental 1933, Milonga brava, Reliquias porteñas) are the standard early-night milonga tanda; Quinteto Pirincho 1950s instrumentals are a separate,
signatureTracks: Yo no sé por qué te quiero (Famá 1934)

name: Osvaldo Fresedo
notes: Smooth, harp and vibraphone; low physical, medium emotional. Best for warm-up with experienced dancers, breathing tandas, and the sweet ending. Instrumentals 1930s-40s (El once, Arrabalero, Vida mía 1933) excellent. Few milongas; valses light. Best: 1933-1939 Ray, 1939-1942 Ruiz, 1940s instrumental

name: Edgardo Donato
notes: Playful, jaunty, 1930s; perfect warm-up and afternoon material; valses (Carnaval de mi barrio, La tapera, Luna de arrabal) and milongas (Ella es así, Sacale punta) are joyful early-night lifts. Do not follow with 1950s Di Sarli (style jump). Best: 1932-1936 instrumental, 1936-1942 Lagos/Gavioli

name: Ángel D'Agostino
notes: Vocal tandas (almost no instrumentals). Soft-rhythmic, intimate, 'de barrio' - ideal for the early hour and the sweet ending; many DJs open the night with D'Agostino-Vargas. Café Domínguez (with its spoken intro) is the classic opener. Milongas (Así me gusta a mí, El porteñito) and valses (Esta noche en Buenos Aires) are few but usable. Best: 1940-1946 Vargas

name: Alfredo De Angelis
notes: Tango 'de calesita' (fairground) feel: strong, singable, slightly sweet. The duet valses (Pregonera, Pastora, Flores del alma, A Magaldi) are peak vals tandas worldwide. Instrumentals 1950s (Pavadita, El tango club) good middle. Milongas few. Best: 1944-1951 Dante/Martel, 1950s instrumental

name: Pedro Laurenz
notes: Bandoneon-led, rhythmic-lyrical, sophisticated; instrumentals (Arrabal 1937, Amurado 1940, Milonga de mis amores 1937) excellent middle; vocal Podestá 1940-41 and Bermúdez. Milonga de mis amores and Yo soy de Parque Patricios are milonga staples. Best: 1937-1941, 1943-1946 Bermúdez

name: Lucio Demare
notes: Piano-led, intimate, slow-lyrical; vocal tandas only (Malena, Mañana zarpa un barco, Tal vez será su voz). Second half of the night / sweet ending; too soft for warm-up or peak. Few milongas and valses; use as a tango-only orchestra. Best: 1938-1943 Miranda, 1943-1945 Berón

name: Francisco Lomuto
notes: Guardia Vieja / early-40s jaunty; instrumentals 1930s and Díaz/Omar vocals; valses and milongas early-night; can be mixed with Canaro/OTV instrumentals of the same years in a 'Guardia Vieja' tanda. Milongas limited. Best: 1930-1936, 1938-1943 Omar

name: Roberto Firpo
notes: Instrumentals, especially the 1930s Cuarteto (El amanecer 1936 with birdsong, Alma de bohemio); charming, light; warm-up and afternoon only; milongas (Milonga orillera) and valses fine for a Guardia Vieja slot. Best: 1927-1939 orquesta/cuarteto

name: Orquesta Típica Victor
notes: Studio orchestra of RCA Victor; crisp 1930s instrumentals (Ventarrón, Sentimiento criollo, Coquetona) and 1935-38 Vargas vocals; valses (Temo, Cuando estaba enamorado) good for the first hour. Reasonable to mix with Canaro/Lomuto in a GV tanda. Best: 1929-1934 instrumental, 1935-1938 Vargas

name: Alfredo Gobbi
notes: Pugliese-adjacent, violin-led; instrumentals (Racing Club 1949, El andariego, Orlando Goñi, Camandulaje) for experienced floors late; difficulty high; one tanda max, rare. Best: 1947-1956 instrumental

name: Ricardo Malerba
notes: Light-rhythmic, bandoneon-driven, singable; one Medina tanda (Embrujamiento, Remembranza, Gitana rusa, Cuando florezcan las rosas) mid-night; valses limited. Best: 1941-1945 Medina

name: Domingo Federico
notes: Ex-Caló bandoneonist; 1943-45 Vidal sides (Al compás de un tango, Yuyo verde, Percal, Tristezas de la calle Corrientes) make one solid middle tanda; valses limited. Best: 1943-1945 Vidal

name: Héctor Varela
notes: D'Arienzo's ex-bandoneonist: keeps a D'Arienzo beat with a spacious Di Sarli-like sound (Brown). 1950s hi-fi; one tanda for the 1950s-flavoured middle/late; milongas (Azúcar, pimienta y sal 1958) and valses fine. Sometimes 'glossy'; most dancers prefer D'Arienzo/Di Sarli. Best: 1952-1958 Ledesma/Lesica, 1950s instrumental

name: Fulvio Salamanca
notes: D'Arienzo's pianist 1940-57; own rhythmic orchestra from 1957 (singer years to verify). Replaces the phantom 'Carlos Salamanca' entry that never merged with the catalogue id.

name: Osmar Maderna
notes: Ex-Caló pianist; delicate, 'Chopin of tango'; instrumentals Lluvia de estrellas, Concierto en la luna (concert-ish, borderline); vocal Verri tandas (Que nunca me falte, Pequeña) for a late, refined slot. Difficulty medium-high. Best: 1946-1950

name: Francini-Pontier
notes: Ex-Caló members; rich 1945-50 arrangements (Brown: 'overblown arrangements tire quickly' - so one tanda); Podestá 1945-47 (Margo, Mañana iré temprano) and Rufino sides; instrumentals A los amigos, Margo for a late refined tanda. Best: 1945-1950

name: Florindo Sassone
notes: Di Sarli-influenced grand 1960s-70s stereo instrumentals ('Bien milonguero' vols. 1-2): fidelity high but the beat is submerged (Brown); use at most one late tanda for a lush floor (Bahía Blanca, El amanecer, Félicia 1960s versions). Low priority. Best: 1958-1975 instrumental

name: José Basso
notes: Troilo-lineage pianist; 1947-50 Fiorentino/Durán sides are danceable; later recordings concert-ish. One late tanda for Troilo-style lovers; verify tracks. Best: 1947-1952

name: Donato Racciatti
notes: Uruguayan D'Arienzo-style; square, bright 1950s hi-fi; good 'D'Arienzo substitute' milongas and valses with female singers (unusual, pleasant). One tanda early/middle. Best: 1950-1960

name: Astor Piazzolla
notes: Concert music; not for the social floor at traditional milongas. The 1946-48 orquesta típica sides (Se armó, Chiclana, El recodo) are danceable, rhythmic and rarely played. At alternative events: Oblivion, Adiós Nonino, Libertango late. Never as cortina. Best: 1946-1948 orquesta típica

name: Horacio Salgán
notes: Sophisticated, syncopated; 1950 orquesta sides (Del 1 al 5, A fuego lento) and Quinteto Real are concert pieces; one late tanda at an 'escucha' event at most. Low priority for the engine. Best: 1950-1957 orquesta

name: Sexteto Mayor
notes: Show tango (Tango Pasión); fast, theatrical (Brown); 'Tangos para bailar' album is the most danceable; occasional late tanda at festivals aimed at stage-tango fans. Rare. Best: Tangos para bailar

name: Color Tango
notes: Pugliese-style with a steady dance beat ('Con estilo de bailar' vols. 1-3; Brown: outstanding). The standard contemporary 'Pugliese substitute' at festivals; same placement rules as Pugliese (late, once). Best: Con estilo de bailar

name: Sexteto Milonguero
notes: Modern vocal sexteto recreating 1940s danceable repertoire (Café Domínguez, Tres esquinas); appears in festival tandas. One tanda in a 4-hour festival night, first half. Not at BsAs-codes milongas. Best: Pa' que bailen (2007-2012)

name: Orquesta Romántica Milonguera
notes: Hi-fi crooning recreations (Di Sarli/Caló flavour, bolero-tinged); hugely popular with newer dancers 2018-2026, divisive with milongueros. Max one tanda per night, first half or sweet ending; never at traditional BsAs milongas. Best: 2016-2024 albums

name: Solo Tango Orquesta
notes: Russian orquesta típica playing faithful D'Arienzo/Di Sarli/Biagi arrangements in hi-fi; danceable; used at festivals as a D'Arienzo substitute; one tanda, first half or main build. Best: 2012-2023 albums

name: Gotan Project
notes: Tango-electrónico; La revancha del tango (2001): Queremos paz, Una música brutal, Época work for alternative floors; 'many dancers have tired of it' (Brown). Alternative preset only; never at a traditional milonga; never next to Pugliese; follow with a milonga or vals. Best: La revancha del tango (2001)

name: Bajofondo
notes: Club layers strong (Brown); En mi/Soledad has the clearest tango pulse; Naranjo en flor works as a slow milonga; Supervielle tracks (Perfume, Pulso) lounge-tango. Alternative preset only. Best: Bajofondo Tango Club (2002), Supervielle (2005)

name: Tanghetto
notes: Lounge-jazz layer on club tango; tracks sound alike; Una llamada and Inmigrante are the dance picks (Brown). Alternative preset only. Best: Emigrante (2003)

name: Otros Aires
notes: Samples old recordings over beats; many tracks work but blur together (Brown: spread across the night, not in a row - but a tanda must be one artist, so pick 3 contrasting tracks). Milonga sentimental is a usable alternative milonga. Alternative preset only. Best: Otros Aires (2004), Dos (2007)

name: Narcotango
notes: Strongest tango sensibility among fusion acts (Brown): Vi luz y subí, Otra luna. Alternative preset only; the gentlest electro option, good as the single alternative tanda late at a mixed event. Best: Narcotango (2003)

name: Miguel Villasboas
notes: Uruguayan 'milonguero' style, square and bouncy; milongas excellent (Villasboas milonga tandas are a festival staple); one tanda early/middle. Best: 1960s-1990s

name: Juan Cambareri
notes: Very fast virtuoso quartet (Brown: 'many very fast cuts'); one milonga or tango tanda for a strong floor at the peak; not for beginners. Best: 1952-1957

name: Francisco Rotundo
notes: Secondary 1950s lyrical orchestra (Ruiz, Campos, Sosa). One tanda in the middle of a long night at most; never the opener or the última.

name: Juan Sánchez Gorio
notes: Rhythmic 1950s orchestra in the D'Arienzo mould; filler for the build phase of long nights, never opener or peak.
